To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) the most stable structures of SnH(2), SnH(4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 14, 16, 18, 20), SnH(22), SnH(26, 30), and SnH(32) are segregated slabs at moderate pressures, (ii) the slabs contain layers of hydrogen and tin atoms, (iii) the slabs are formed from the elements in the β-Sm,
(i) the ground-state of SnH(2) is a layered structure, and (ii) this layered structure persists up to moderate pressures, where it is replaced by a structure with higher coordination.

(i) the most stable structure of SnH(2) at 0 K and ambient pressure is a layered structure, with tin atoms in the bcc arrangement and hydrogen atoms in the molecular form, and (ii) at high pressure, the most stable structure is a simple mixture of the elements, Sn and H(2).
In summary, our research is concerned with
structural instability under pressure.
the thermodynamic stability of the elements, and with the structural instability of compounds that are kinetically stable but thermodynamically unstable.

the general problem of the thermodynamic instability of molecular compounds with respect to the element(s) and the formation of layered structures as a compromise between electronic and thermodynamic factors.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
, in the case of SnH(,4), the pressure-induced structural changes are dominated by the tendency of tin to form a metallic phase and hydrogen to form a molecular phase.
the pressure-induced decomposition of SnH( 4) into the elements is preceded by segregation of Sn and H into layers.

the pressure-induced decomposition into the elements is not a general problem for thermodynamically unstable molecular compounds, and that the formation of segregated layers is not a necessary consequence of such instability.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the ground-state structures of SnH(,4) are layered at moderate pressures, but become 3D at high pressure.
the layered structures of SnH(3) and SnH(2) are the most stable at 50 GPa, while at 140 GPa the structures with the largest coordination numbers are most stable.
, for SnH(4)-like systems, the pressure-induced structural changes are more complex than previously anticipated.
The main takeaway from our work is that
segregated layers are a general feature for compounds that are thermodynamically unstable with respect to the constituent elements.

the structural instability of SnH( 4) under pressure can be explained by the formation of a segregated layer of tin atoms in a β-Sn configuration, and that the same mechanism can be expected to apply for a large class of unstable molecular compounds.
segregated layers of elements may be a common feature in the high-pressure structures of thermodynamically unstable compounds.
